M.r. HERRON. I wish to draw the attention of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), and I had hoped also that of the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver), but I am sorry to see that the Minister of the Interior is not in his seat, to a matter that has come to my attention in connection with the supply of seed grain to settlers in the Northwest. I received a communication to-day from a settler in my constituency complaining of the quality and cost of the seed grain supplied by the government to settlers in that vicinity. I have here a sample of the wheat which was supplied, and I suppose that the sample would be one which would appeal more particularly to the Minister of Agriculture. I have -also a complaint with reference to the price. As I understand this grain is supplied through the Department of the Interior, and their officials in the Northwest, and the complaint made to me is to the effect that this wheat, laid down at Gleichen, a station on the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway near Calgary, at a cost of $1.25 per bushel is of a rather inferior grade, and from my own knowledge of wheat, grading and price, I would say
that it would grade probably No. 2 Northern, and not more than that if it was clean which it is not. It is tainted very badly. with weed seeds. I am not capable of judging whether they are of the noxious kind or not, but I presume they are. The wheat is mixed very badly with weed seeds. For the last two or three years wheat of this quality has been sold at the stations in the locality where this wheat is supplied at 75 cents, or at the most, 80 cents a bushel. It seems to me that this is entirely too much to pay for that quality of seed wheat. My correspondent has not given me very full information regarding the seed. Whether it was purchased in Manitoba, or in some of the western provinces, or in Ontario, I have no means of judging. But I think that the two points which I have mentioned, quality and price are worthy of consideration. I shall be glad to hand over the sample to the Minister of Agriculture, and see if he would not consider that it was very injurious to the interests of the Northwest to have seed of that quality supplied and distributed among the farmers of that country. I think the Minister of the Interior would be justified in investigating closely the price charged because, as far as I am capable of judging, it is much above the standard price.

As this seed is distributed to the settlers with whom the Department of the Interior is in close touch, the whole work in connection with the distribution is managed by the Department of the Interior.
I have not, therefore, the information at my command at the moment to reply to the hon. gentleman, but I would be very glad if he would let me have a sample of the seed he has, and I would consult with my colleague, the Minister of the Interior, and investigate the matter.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Fisheries Act, chapter 45 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, he amended by enacting that in the province of British Columbia" no one shall engage in the manufacture of oil or other commercial products from sea-lions, hair seals, sharks or dog-fish, nor operate a salmon cannery or salmon curing establishment, except under license from the minister; that the site of reduction works must be approved by the minister ; that operations must proceed within one year from issue of the license for which annual fees shall be required; that the annual fees for a lobster fishing license be increased and based on the total number of pounds of canned lobsters; that the annual returns to the minister by the owner or manager of a lobster factory, through the inspector of fisheries oif the district, shall furnish more details and be submitted not later than the 31st day of
May, each year, and penalties for failure to make such returns shall he imposed; and that licenses unust he obtained for maintaining lobster pounds, with an annual fee for the same.-iMr. Brodeur.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. P. BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries).
speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
In this resolution we first ask for a provision authorizing the government to enact that in British Columbia no one shall engage in the manufacture of oil or other commercial products from sea lions, hair seals, sharks, or dog-fish, without taking out a license. from the department. This has been asked by some people who are willing to take up that industry. So far nothing has been done with regard to the reduction of sea lions and similar mammals. I think we should encourage any person or company willing to start works for the purpose of destroying those mammals, which are a menace to the food fish generally. It has been suggested to us that such a thing could not be done unless we could establish regulations by which the reduction works could be established at a certain distance, one from the other, in order to give each factory an area large enough to ensure a catch which would maintain the reduction works. We have now similar legislation in regard to the whale fisheries, no whale reducing works may be established within a certain distance of an existing reduction works. By having power to license reduction works we can at the same time determine the area within which they may fish and the distance at which other works may be established. This legislation has worked very satisfactorily in connection with the whale fisheries. We are now asked to apply the same regulations to reduction works on the British Columbia coast for the handling of sea * lions, hair seals, sharks and dog-fish. The fee proposed is a nominal one, $1. I think there should be no objection to that proposal.
The second proposal is to authorize the government to impose a license upon salmon canning or salmon curing establishments. Some years ago we had in British Columbia a very extensive commission which inquired into the whole question of fisheries in that province. That commission recommended that the salmon canning establishments should be licensed, and the owners of these establishments have themselves asked for the imposition of a license. The license fee proposed is $50. This license is the result of the unanimous recommendation of the commission, and it is accepted, as I have said, by the cannery establishments themselves.
The other change is with regard to the annual fee for lobster fishing establishments. This proposal is the result of the report and recommendation of the Committee on Marine and Fisheries last year. Lobster fishing licenses were the subject of a great Mr. FISHER.
deal of discussion in the maritime provinces. For years there were complaints that the regulations were not sufficient and that amendments should be made. The House referred the whole question to the Committee on Marine and Fisheries. The committee sat during the session of 1909. A very long inquiry was then made by the committee, and they suggested to the government that during the recess a commissioner should be appointed to visit the different portions oi the maritime provinces and continue the investigation, securing especially the evidence of the fishermen. Dr. Wakeham was appointed to make this investigation. He went through all the maritime provinces and made a report, which has been submitted to the Committee on Marine and Fisheries. The committee at the end of last session recommended some changes in our regulations. These changes have all been carried out by an order in council passed in September last, which - was amended some months later with regard to a certain feature. The commission recommended the increase in the licenses which I am now proposing.
To what extent is the industry of manufacturing oil from dogfish carried on?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: In the maritime provinces we have dog-fish reduction works exploited by the government at three places. But in the province of British Columbia there are to-day no dog-fish reduction works, properly speaking.

Will the minister give us some information with regard to the dog-fish reduction works in the maritime provinces-how they are carried on, what is the general result, and under whose charge are they being conducted?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: In the maritime provinces there are three places where dog-fish reduction works are being carried on- Canso, Shippigan and Clark's Harbour. At each of these places we have an establishment under the control of a superintendent. We purchase the dog-fish from the fishermen, and from them produce two by-products, oil and fertilizer. The fertilizer is offered for sale at a very low price to the farmers, and any balance that is left is advertised for sale. The same procedure is followed with regard to the oil, which we sell at the price offered to us.

Is it the intention of the department, after this system is introduced, to offer a bonus for the establishment of works for the manufacture of oil as it did for the establishment of the fertilizer works?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
We are not proposing any bonus, because we hope that the people

who are willing to go into the business may make it a success, as in the case of the whale fisheries.

The reason I ask is that it is very essential to the prosperity of the fisheries m British Columbia, particularly those in the vicinity of the Fraser river, that such works should be encouraged. The sea-lions particularly are increasing there to such an extent that the object which the minister has in view will not be accomplished if there are only one or two of these reduction works, or if the work is carried on on a limited scale with the idea of making a profit for the proprietors rather than with the idea of giving the utmost freedom in the reduction of these pests to the salmon fisheries. If the hon. minister had the authority, he might do as he has done in the case of the salmon fisheries, so restrict the number of licenses as to create a monopoly, which has not operated to the best interests of the industry. I would like to hear the minister say in this connection that he will not re' strict the number of these places, but that subject to the proper regulation every person who wishes to engage in this industry shall have an equal chance with every other person.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I agree with my hon. friend that it is very important that some of these reduction works should be successful, as these dog-fish and sea-lions are a great nuisance to the salmon fisheries. The intention of the department is not to restrict these establishments in such a way that there would not be a sufficient number of works to deal with all the dog-fish that might be found in some localities. I know that in the locality my hon. friend has mentiohed this pest has caused considerable disturbance to the salmon fishery, and I am willing to take the necessary steps to encourage any establishment for its reduction.
This clause refers also to the licenses of the salmon canneries and salmon-curing establishments. Does it differ in any respect from the present regulations governing the salmon fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Not at all. There was some doubt as to whether or not it would be necessary to have regulations to authorize us to collect these sums, and this is to give us power for that purpose.
Are the dogfish on the Pacific coast similar to those on the coasts of the maritime provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, they are supposed to belong to the same species.

I understand that scientific authority as well as individual taste
have decided that dog-fish is an excellent food. Of course the finest way of getting rid of dog-fish is to make it a popular article of diet, so that fish dealers and fish eaters will be spurred to activity to exterminate the species. The times change in that respect; a few years ago the suggestion to eat sword-fish would be treated something like a suggestion to eat the swords themselves, but sword-fish to-day is a somewhat luxurious food and sells at a high price. Dog-fish are most disreputable looking animals when you see them, and when you put them through a process which is not curative, they are worse than ill looking; but if dog-fish are good to eat you have solved the problem of their continued existence. Has the minister made any efforts to educate public opinion up to getting dogfish off the index expurgatorius and put on the edible list.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I understand that efforts were made some years ago to can dogfish, but those engaged in the industrv put them on the market labelled as whitefish, and although we had no legislative authority to prevent that we discouraged it, in the fear that it would compete with the excellent whitefish of the Great Lakes, and give our excellent whitefish a bad name. I should mention, however, that the intention of those who engaged in the trade was not to sell the dog-fish in Canada, but in a foreign market. Since we have established dog-fish reduction works to make oil and fertilizer, the fishermen who formerly disposed of dog-fish for canning find a ready market for it at the reduction work's, and that no doubt has some influence on the discontinuance of the experiment.

I would suggest to the minister that you might almost as well hang a man as give him a bad name, and when you set up a public enterprise for turning dog-fish into manure no decent Christian wants to have anything to do with a fish that seems to be fit only for that particular purpose. I would suggest that the minister should change the name and call it, say, Pisces Canadensis, and start it off with some fair chance of making a'success of itself. Has the minister himself ever eaten any dog-fish?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No.

I have no doubt the minister is prejudiced against it because it is called dog-fish, and you might just as well call it some other name because no one wants to eat dog if he knows it. The scientists say it is a fine fish and it teems in our waters. Why, if you were to see a shoal of dog-fish after you, down off Grand Manan, you would run more quickly than if you were in the Niobe with a hostile

fleet chasing you. The minister should, I think, take away the bad name of the thing and give it a start in life, or rather in death.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Dog-fish is of course inferior as compared with our other commercial fishes, and being destructive of the superior fish we started reduction works to make some economic use of the dog-fish and to diminish their numbers.
Mr.FRASER. Did the whitefish suffer in competition with the dog-fish?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No. The whitefish is a product of the Great Lakes and is not found on the Atlantic coast, so that there was no competition between them. But the canned dog-fish were put on the market under the name of whitefish.
Not by the department.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Oh, no; quite the contrary. Some one started in the maritime provinces an establishment for canning dogfish and they labelled it as whitefish.
Mr. FOSTER, I really think the minister might arrange it in this way:	There
are practically no whitefish in the maritime provinces. There are a few in some of the lakes, but they are not a commercial quantity. If a fisherman goes up through the lakes and spends a fortnight, he may get enough whitefish to feed him for that time. These fish can never compete with the whitefish of Manitoba, nor would they be likely to compete with the whitefish in Ontario. But let the minister give them some other name-say: 'Sea Whitefish' or ' Maritime Whitefish,' and let them go.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: But foreign countries which purchase our fish will not be able to make the distinction between sea white-fish and the other.
Foreign countries do net buy our whitefish.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, they are being sold in foreign markets-in the United States they are sold in large quantities. Besides, this is not within our jurisdiction. We have nothing in the law which would authorize us to give the fish a particular name. So far as that is concerned we have no inspection law. It is much to be desired that we should have inspection law, and that is a matter which is engaging, I understand the consideration of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
I would have the fishery experts make a thorough investigation of it. Let us understand the quality and see if anything can be done.

I think if the hon. member for North Toronto
. Mr. FOSTER.
(Mr. Foster) could see and smell the dogfish of British Columbia waters the fish would lose a champion, and I do not think that by any other name it could be made to smell sweeter. For the information of the hon. gentleman I may explain that dogfish are not regarded on the Pacific coast as valuable except by the Japanese, and they will not use them if they can get any other fish. Any measure the minister can take for the extermination of the dog-fish will be very heartily welcomed by those engaged in the fisheries, on the Pacific coast. I would like to ask, going back to the section in connection with the licenses for salmon canneries or salmon curing establishments, whether the minister proposes to m-ake under these regulations a uniform fee for establishments of whatever capacity, or whether he has it in mind to accede to the request of petitioners to him that exception should be made in favour of establishments, curing establishments particularly, carried on in a semiprivate way by one or two fishermen. I may remind him, that, as I am informed, he has been petitioned on this subject, and it has been represented to him that hardships are worked on men who wish to cure fish within their own establishments by compelling them to take out a license and pay a fee equal to that paid by a large establishment.

Before the question of the dog-fish is passed, I would like to say a word or two on behalf of that fish. I have had some experience with the dog-fish on my own table and in other homes. I consider the dog-fish one of the best edible fishes we have. Its flesh is fine in appearance, and is of excellent taste, comparing, I think, with the salmon. There is nothing against the dog-fish except its very nasty n-ame, given to it by some ignorant fishermen. It is a bad thing to have a bad name, as some people know, and its bad name is the only thing that I know of- except its lack of beauty-that is the matter with the dog-fish. I have had it served to guests at my table without letting them know what it was; and after receiving high encomiums on its taste I have told them it was dog-fish-and then they were sorry they had breakfasted. But we have no better food fish in our waters, in my opinion, than the dog-fish. Its liver is very valuable for the production of oil which is equal to cod liver oil for medicinal purpose's, and its yield is to cod as five to one. The odour of the oil of the dog-fish liver is bad, but that odour is very easily taken out, so that dog-fish liver oil and cod liver oil cannot be distinguished one from the other.

I would like to ask a question. Am I right in thinking, in refer-

ence to the oil taken from the dog-fish, that it is not suffused through the flesh of the animal, but is in the liver?

I have never noticed any rank taste in the flesh. It is an oily fish, but the oil in the liver is not that in the flesh. If it was not for the name, it would be a food fish, there is no doubt. It is something like our Intercolonial railway, which was named by foreigners before confederation, a railway between ' the colonies ' of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec-' don't you know '-and the name has stuck to it ever since. I am afraid it has been a hoodoo to it all along.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: In answer to the question of my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor), it is not our intention to fix different license fees for different sorts of canneries. The fee of $50 seems to be a very small one, and I think could be paid by all the canneries that will be established.

I think the minister does not understand. I referred to the inclusion of salmon canning and salmon curing establishments in the same sentence. I speak particularly of salmon curing, which, as the minister knows, is different from canning. A man may carry on salmon curing in his back shed, but not salmon canning. I know the case of a man who attempted to carry on salmon curing in his own premises on a domestic scale, simply by his own labour, and was confronted with a demand for a heavy license fee, the same as if he had a large commercial establishment. It is on behalf of the salmon curer that I wras appealing to the minister, and I think his case is deserving of consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: This is the first time, I think, that the matter has been brought seriously to my attention. I will look into it and see if it is desirable to make the changes to meet the cases mentioned. But I believe the hon. gentleman will admit with me that it is important that we should have some control over these establishments, and the only way we can do it is by license.

That is correct, but it is a hardship -for these men who have facilities for curing to be told that they must not carry on this operation unless they pay a prohibitive license fee. I would like to refer again to the restriction of the number of establishments. I understood the minister to say that it is not the intention to make any change in the present regulations as to salmon canning. If il understand it, there is a restriction in the number of salmon canning licenses, which works out in this way-the men presently engaged in the salmon canning have formed themselves into an absolutely close corporation and no person aggrieved by the operations of the combine can start any new establishment, because when he applies for a license he is informed by the local officials that the policy of the department is to give no more licenses. The department takes the ground that it is not to the advantage of the industry to have a greater number of canneries. While an argument may be made on that score, yet the minister will see that when, in the only field of production of this class of salmon, he limits the licenses to persons already having canneries and licenses, he creates a monopoly. -I would like to ask him whether he is prepared to make his regulations more elastic, and to consider each application for a license on its own merits, without regard to whether or not that man has been in the business before.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend will see by the regulations we have passed on regard to the canneries that the public is absolutely protected. If there was any suspicion, or any ground for a monopoly by which the fishermen could be in any way affected, of course we are authorized to issue other licenses. But it was represented to the commission, when the commission sat in British Columbia, that the number of canneries which were then existing on the Fraser river especially was large enough. I do not know whether that is correct, my hon. friend is more familiar than I am with the condition of affairs there. He can tell the committee whether he thinks the number of establishments there is sufficient or not. At all events, that was the report made by the commission, and as a result we acceded to the request that no more licenses should be given, on one condition, namely, that if we found that there is a strong suspicion of a monopoly existing, we will certainly exercise the power we have of giving new licenses in order to prevent a monopoly which would be detrimental to the industry itself.

The minister doubtless knows that at present there is a monopoly, whether bad or ill, I will not discuss now; but there is an absolute monopoly of the salmon canning industry in British Columbia, allied with the Alaska salmon canners, thus creating an industry protected on all sides by the government that is, perhaps the most profitable industry in connection with fisheries any where in the world. The profits are very large, very easily and quickly made, and with very little risk. I know that the fishermen are subjected to injustice on the Canadian side because of the

existence of this monopoly. We think we are superior to the United States in the matter of monopolies and trusts, but they must yield the palm to us in connection with the -salmon fisheries. On the Washington side the monopoly is not so complete, as there are quite a few of what are known as independent canneries, which are always available to fishermen who wish to sell their catch to them. The effect on the Washington side is to make the price to fishermen very much larger than it would be otherwise. I do not think that -any person except those making financial profits by this operation would suggest to the minister that the fisheries are protected in -any way by restriction in the number of licenses to foe issued, and there is no reason to suppose that there would be any greater number of fishermen, or any greater quantity of salmon caught, if there were more^ canneries than there are at present. I do not suggest that there are not enough canneries to can all the -fish to be caught along the Fraser river, because it is the work of a very short time to duplicate or to increase to an indefinite quantity the. capacity of any cannery. But since no new person can get a canning license, the minister fosters a monopoly which works detrimentally to the men who ought to get whatever benefit may be legitimately derived as their reward for catching the fish.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I am surprised to hear that there is a monopoly in the Fraser river. My hon. friend is aware that so far as the Fraser river is concerned, there is an association called the British Columbia Packers' Association which is a very large one. I do not know whether it is successful financially.
They are getting on very well indeed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I always understood that of course they are controlling a very large number of canneries on the Fraser river, but there are also -some independent canneries. I do not know whether the independent canneries -are as large as those under the control of this association.

The independent canneries to which the minister refers -are largely the work of Scotch capital. The independent packers' and the British Columbia Packers' Association are combined in another association called the Fraser River Canners' Association, which includes both the British Columbia Packers' and those he terms the independent canners.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: My hon. friend says that all those canneries are in that association.
They are all in the Fraser River Canners' Association.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That is not the information we have in the department.
They control the buying price and the selling price.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The information we have in the department is to the effect that there is a British Columbia Canners' Association, and outside of that .an independent canneries, and of course the general association of which my hon. friend speaks, the Fraser River Canners' Association. The information we have in the department is to the effect that all the canning establishments of the Fraser river are not included. I am glad the hon. gentleman has brought this matter to my attention, and we will look into it.

I would like to make it plain to the minister that the Fraser River Canners' Association is not an investing association at all, but it is an association in which the British Columbia Packers' Association, the great organization there, combined with the independent canners under the name of the Fraser River Canners' Association, with their separate officers.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I thought the Fraser River Canners' Association had disappeared, and became merged into the British Columbia Canners' Association.

No, it is the other way about. The British Columbia Packers' Association was organized with Toronto capital, by Henry Doyle, seven or eight years ago. Outside of that, the canneries controlled by the Bell-Irving interests have continued to exist, and there is also the St. Mungo cannery' on the Fraser river, established by Scotch capital, and which never sold out to the British Columbia Packers. But they are all joined to -form the Fraser River Canners' Association, with a paid secretary and an office in Vancouver. From that central office all these canners fix the price at which they will buy and sell their salmon. They are allied with the Alaska Packers' Association and with the operators of the canneries on Puget Sound. The proprietor of several canneries on Puget Sound is the manager of the British Columbia Packers' Association. The minister will see that there is an absolutely close ring-I was going to say, but that is regarded as an offensive term.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Cordiality.

Yes, an absolutely close association so that

they can impose whatever condition they like upon the fishermen as respects the price of fish, and the quantity to be taken. That is another point which might well engage the minister's attention.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Who is the secretary of this British Columbia Canners' Association?
My last information was that it was Mr. W. D. Burdis, of Vancover. He has been secretary of the Fraser River Canners' Association for several years. I have not heard of any change.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
The information we
had in the department was that Mr. Burdis was secretary of the Fraser River [DOT]Canners' Association, but that it had changed its name to the British Columbia Canners' Association.
Was that this year?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
About a couple of
years ago.

I got a circular from them last year and my information is certainly direct up to the close of last year. They have an absolutely close buying and selling combine. It is well known to all engaged in the business out there. Another way that the minister's kindness to this monopoly affects the fishermen is this: When there is more than the ordinary run of fish jour fishermen are absolutely prohibited from getting any advantage from that by title limitation placed bv these canners. upon the number they will take from each boat. As the minister knows, no other canners are allowed to come in, and no>
other licenses are issued. There are no canneries in reserve to be opened up if there is a glut of fish. There comes an extraordinary run,' and every man out fishing will receive 500 of 600 fish in his boat, but when he goes to the cannery wharf he receives notice, and it is the same with every cannery, that the managers have placed a limit of 200 to each boat. That means that they can sell 200 to the canners and must absolutely destroy the other 400. The fisherman cannot even throw the fish into the river because that is against the law.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
Could he not sell them to the independent canners?
Mr. TAYLOR ' /New Westminster). There are no independent canners because they are all in this buying and selling combine. On the American side he can sell them to the independent canners, but on , the Canadian side he can not. The result is that the fisherman is at the loss of all these fish, and the community loses this
valuable product which has to be destroyed because of the regulation of the canners. That goes on every season, and it is the cause of very great heart burning to the fisherman that after he has made an exceptionally large catch he finds that he is deprived by his government of any opportunity of selling the fish he has caught.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: That is a matter over which we have no control except by way of granting new licenses. We have the power to grant new licenses. If we found that the Fraser river could stand more canneries, and that fishermen were obliged to destroy their fish we would be willing to consider very seriously the granting of new licenses. But, as to the refusal of some of the canners to take more than a certain quantity of fish, that is a matter over which we have no control.

Granting for the sake of argument that there is absolutely no monopoly, I would like to hear from the minister what he considers the advantage to be in leaving to a certain number the privilege and right to enjoy a natural resource such as that of our fisheries. It is the encouragement of monopolies of that kind that starts the growth of those enormous trusts that have been of such vital injury to the United States. Not only do these monopolies exist with respect to the fisheries, but with respect to timber and all natural resources of that kind. What is the supposed advantage? Why should I not be able to go down there without any question at all, merely as a matter of absolute right under the statute, and say that I want a license, tender my money and get it? Why should ten men have the right to erect canneries, and the eleventh man be shut out in a supposed free country such as this? What are the reasons for such a regulation?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
These regulations have been framed upon the report of the Fisheries Commission which sat a .couple of years ago, and came to the conclusion that such regulations were in the interests of the fisheries. It may be that the argument of my hon. friend would apply just as well to the ease of our regulations generally, or to the restrictions which we have made with regard to the preservation of the fisheries. We adopt regulations for what purpose? For the purpose of protecting the fisheries, for the purpose of preventing the destruction of what I consider a national asset. It was represented to us that if the number of car-neries was larger than the requirements of the Fraser river it would mean that perhaps at some future time, not very far distant, the fisheries there would be destroyed. This is a measure which has

been adopted for the purpose of protecting the fisheries, but if the fisheries are not treated fairly by these canners, we have the power, under the existing regulations, to prevent any such injustice being done to the fishermen by granting new licenses. Every man will have to apply, and his case will be considered.

The minister has not answered the argument at all. As he has said, he has made general regulations for the fisheries, and if that is so the whole country should be treated alike. In this particular case the canners already in business, and who are supposed to know the conditions advise the commission that it would be in the interest of the fisheries to adopt these regulations. Of course they give that advice, and it would be very foolish of them not to. That is the whole argument of the minister now. Then he says that if he finds that those who are in the business now are not able to take all the fish, he may consider the question of letting somebody else in. As my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has pointed out, it is an easy matter for the canners already established to enlarge, double or quadruple their capacity, and still hold the monopoly. It is not only unfair to the people of Canada, but it is the very beginning of the most vicious system that it is possible to introduce into any country. The evil of this system has been pointed out by your own Dominion Conservation Commission, and I think that one of the first duties of that commission is to direct attention to this grave danger to the people of Canada. If you take this very question now, the whole cry, from the President down, is that they, through monopoly, have practically destroyed and wasted the natural resources of the United States, and the argument of the minister this afternoon is exactly that argument. I am taking a general stand regardless of details, not going into that question at all, that it is a very vicious system whereby you allow a limited number of men to have the absolute, and sole right of such an enormously profitable industry, and a natural resource that belongs to the people as a whole, a food producer as is suggested by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Crosby) who is vitally interested.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) has made out an absolute case. I was down last summer and he had the courtesy and kindness to drive me around to see some of the canneries which were open. Some of them were closed down as it was towards the end of the season. He called my attention to fishermen coming there bringing fish and at that time, he said, unfortunately these canneries were Mr. BRODETTR.
not taking all the fish of these men, only a limited number because there were too many offering, there happened to be an extra late run, they were getting a large number of fish, some of which were being destroyed. That should not be allowed, the regulations should be absolutely general. You cannot place this industry on a par with liquor licenses where there is considered to be a certain evil and, therefore, you limit the traffic, that does not apply here. Here is a food for the people at large, a natural resource belonging to the people, and you say to a certain limited number of men, I do not care whether it is a monopoly or not, that they shall have the sole right to carry on this industry. They thus get established, they grow stronger every season, they accumulate more wealth and power to build up the very trusts which are recognized as an evil in every country in the world, and which we are endeavouring to fight against. I claim that it is the duty of the minister not only to take it into his serious consideration, but absolutely to have free trade as far as establishing these canneries' is concerned. My hon. friend has made that point clear in regard to curing. He points out: Here is an individual fisherman with enterprise who by frugality and industry has got an extra boat or has been successful and undertakes to cure a few fish and start to build up an industry. That is the way we have built up all our industries throughout Canada. But immediately the regulations of the department step in and say to him [DOT] Unless you pay the full license of one of these great trust magnates, you are net allowed to cure a single fish. In other words there is a penalty on their enterprise, and the enterprising fisherman is immediately choked off. That is a fair argument. My objection to the resolution is that it takes over the power to continue that monopoly and increase it. What is. going to be the advantage of a regulation giving certain ones and only certain ones a license to manufacture, for instance, this oil and not allow everybody to enter into that industry? Why have they not all the same free right? Why bring in a resolution providing for an enactment to place them in exactly the same position as you have already placed the fish canning and curing industry? In other words, you are going to make a complete monopoly of the fisheries of British Columbia. The individual fisherman cannot can or cure and now you take power to enact that no man can make oil unless he gets a license, and thus to make a hard and fast, hidebound monopoly of fishing in British Columbia. What is the ground for the proposed monopoly? The hon. member for New Westminster has pointed out exactly how it works and is bound to work

on the general principle and I object to that principle because it is vicious.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext:
The principle which we adopted concerning the whale fisheries, which we are now proposing to apply to the sea-lion reduction works is based upon the experience of Newfoundland. Newfoundland some years ago started whale reduction works on a very large scale. There was no restriction at all, every one could go and catch whales in every part of the gulf, and in a few years there were the number of reduction works and the consequent fishing became so extensive that the whale fishing was practically destroyed. In order to avoid a repetition of that in Canada we thought it well to adopt this law which was passed some years ago by which we took power to license the reduction establishments for whales and to declare in the statute that a certain area of the Gulf would be practically at their disposal. Reduction works were established at Seven Islands on the north shore. We would not then allow license to another establishment within 100 miles of Seven Islands. Of course if one was established beyond 100 miles they would have the right to go and fish any place in the Gulf, but that was a restriction that prevented the destruction of whales and promised good financial results to the reduction works themselves. In spite of that protection it was found in a few years that this establishment which was licensed at Seven Islands was not a success financially and it had to close. I am informed, however, that it will likely be reopened very soon. If we had permitted at that time every company to go there and carry on the fishery there would have been no success financially, and besides that we would have destroyed the whales, although, of course, it is not of great importance that the whales should be destroyed On the British Columbia coast there are companies or a company which is applying for permission to reduce sea-lions, hair-seals and sharks. This company is willing to go into business, but they say that if they start business in a certain area then in a few years, when they have made a success, some one else may establish himself alongside of them and they may lose the capital invested. Consequently they ask us to establish regulations by which reduction works would not be established in the same area so that the same thing would happen as in the Gulf. It is thought that with some restriction the companies will likely be successful. This is a new industry which would not be started unless they had this protection which they are seeking. I think it worth while to give them an opportunity to start these works.
That is the reason for the policy we are now introducing.

I cannot see why the principle of the survival of the fittest should not apply there as in the general trade and business of the country. The minister himself said that even when they granted this restriction in the case he named, the industry was not a practical success. He seemed to think that might yet be made a success. There should be a general regulation so that every man would have an equal opportunity. If you insist that it is in the interest of the public to give monopolies of this kind, then you must, to be logical, and in order to secure for the fishermen fair value for their labour, regulate in some way the prices in connection therewith-in other words, regulate the trade. That has certainly not been done, and the neglect to do that leads to the evils that we see on every hand. I do not think that any man who has studied the question fails to realize that the creation of monopolies of this kind has brought about very great and evil results, and that is my chief objection in a general way to this resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: When my hon. friend applies the word 'monopoly' to the legislation now proposed, I must tell him that that expression is absolutely uncalled-for. The regulations will provide that the licenses shall be for every 50 miles of coast. As there are about 7,000 miles of coast in British Columbia, that certainly could not be considered as a monopoly. So far nobody has been willing to go into the business; but some enterprising men are willing to go into it. It may be a failure or it may be a success; we do not know; but they ask us to give to them the same regulations as we are giving with regard to whales, and we think their request is a fair one, and is not to be considered as one for a monopoly.

I am not saying that the resolution itself is a monopoly, but I say that it may lead to a monopoly. I am only pointing out that that has been the practical result in similar cases, in order to warn the hon. minister of the great danger of legislation of this kind, and that it must be very carefully considered. If he finds that there are sufficiently logical reasons advanced for it, then he should be careful to hedge it about with other restrictions and regulations that will protect the general public and the fisheries themselves. I think the hon. member tor New Westminster has laid down the basic principle, which is that the actual producer, and not the manufacturer, if I may use that word, is the one we must protect. It is the million fisher-folk in the North Sea that makes the fisheries valuable there, and it

is the fisher-folk on the Pacific coast that we should carefully protect.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The preservation of the nsn too.

Yes, because without the fish we would not have the fisher-folk. But the great danger is that in protecting the fish you may be protecting men whose interest is to become a trust or a monopoly as against the fisher-folk.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We have the same regulations in British Columbia with regard to the whale fisheries, and so far we have not had sufficient applications for licenses to cover the whole coast.

The minister mentioned a certain application that had been made to him for permission to go into this industry. I would like to know if he has given any promise to those people that no matter who else is refused a license, they will get one.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I never made any such promise.
They are going it blind, then?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes, they are going to apply if this legislation is passed.
And the minister feels in honour bound to give them a license?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Yes.
Then the minister creates a monopoly at once.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Not at all.

Because if you have 7,000 miles of coast line in British Columbia, and one license is allowed for every 50 miles, the minister will not contend that each 50 miles throughout the whole province is of equal value to every other. There must be a choice. For instances, so far as the dog-fish and the sea-otter are concerned, a site that would be infinitely more valuable than any other would be one at the mouth of the Fraser river. Surely the minister has some order of value of these sites. If there are a dozen applications, those persons to whom he has already committed himself will get all the valuable sites, and the rest of us who want to take part in this industry will be told to go away off and choose locations where there are no fish. I think the minister will see that he has told the committee too much, because these regulations are actually laid down to suit certain interests who have promised to go into this business. I think the minister should promise that if he issues- these licenses he will put them up to competition so that everybody will have a chance. The Mr. GOODEVE.
Minister of Marine and Fisheries controls only his own department; but as a member of the government he has to do to a certain extent with other departments, and if he will assure us that regulations of this kind will be acceptable throughout all the departments, that might make a difference to some of us. For instance, I know I have a sympathetic listener in the Minister of Inland Revenue, and I would appeal to him. He and I are engaged in the same' business, that of producing newspapers. We are bothered by the fact that as soon as we get our business established, some other fellow comes into the field and starts another newspaper and cuts down our profits. Besides the extraordinary size of some of these papers is having an appreciable effect on the supply of pulpwood. If the Minister of Inland Revenue could assure us that he would apply to the Department of Trade and Commerce or some other department, or take authority to limit the number of newspapers, so that we might make whatever profits we chose to make, we might look with a more kindly eye on the proposed fishery monopoly. I do not say that we would; but we are all human, and if the minister should tempt us in that way, there is no knowing what might result in the way of softening our opposition to this proposition. But, joking apart, if the minister is going to limit the number of these licenses, he should advertise for tenders for them.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: If two applications were made the proposition of my hon. friend might be very well considered, but we have neveT had more than one application and this did not refer to the Fraser river which my hon. friend does not consider a good place for dog-fish, or sharks, or sea-lions. I do not know a good site would be found at the imouth of the Fraser river, but if an application comes from there it will be considered. My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor), will find that as in the case of the whale fisheries, everybody will be fairly treated and no favouritism shown.
What is the present position of the lobster fisheries in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: We have no lobster canneries so far in British Columbia.
This resolution merely anticipates that there will be lobster fisheries in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It refers to the Atlantic coast, but of course it is a general law for the whole of Canada.

That is what it is intended to be, but I under-

stand the English language and the resolution only applies to British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The Bill itself will remove any doubt on the point.

I have been struck with the logic of the arguments advanced by the bon. gentleman from British Columbia. The minister stated there were about 7,000 miles of coast line in British Columbia, and that he intended to grant a license for each 50 miles. Of course, there must be extents of that coast where it would not be worth while placing a factory in 500 miles for any kind of fishing, and the location of a factory must depend on the conditions as to 'fishing, &c. The fact that you have 7,000 miles of coast would not at all indicate that you would have one applicant for each 50 miles. If an application can be had- to establish an industry on that coast would it not be fair to specify a limited time, say three years, for the /monopoly, if it is to be a monopoly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It is only one year.
That would relieve the difficulty somewhat. I understood the minister to say that in Newfoundland they have restrictions on the whale fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I said quite the contrary, and I believe that is why several reduction works have had to be closed.

When the whale fisheries were first established on the Newfoundland coast and the Newfoundland-LabTador coast, some of those engaged in the industry earned as high as 150 per cent, and some of course earned nothing. People should have an unrestricted opportunity of going into that class of business if they desire to take chances, and I do not think the government need worry itself much about that. The success of the business will depend on the experience, and on the brain and energy that is put into it. When the whale fishery was first established in Newfoundland people were rushing into it with their money just as into a gold mining enterprise, and the chances of gain or loss were about the same. Some became rich, and some lost.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: What percentage became rich?

Some of the Scotch firms that went into the business did well and others failed to succeed. The whale business is not now as profitable as it was because the fish are not now so plentiful as they were formerly. The resolution says that the annual fee for lobster fishing licenses shall be increased and based on the total number of pounds of canned
lobsters. I did not know that there was any charge previously for a lobster fishing license.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The existing legislation provides that the license fee shall be $2 per 100 cases or packages or fraction thereof.
I know that, but what I said, was that I did not understand the lobster fishermen had to get a license.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Lobster establishments have. There is a difference between the lobsteT establishment and the lobster fishermen. The lobster fisherman has no license to can lobsters-that privilege was taken away from him years ago? .
When I asked the minister if the lobster fishermen had to pay a license, he said. ' yes.'	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I misunderstood my hon. friend. The lobster fishermen pays no license.
The resolution is wrong in that particular.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The Bill-

I have before me only the resolution as it appears on the Order Paper, and that is what we are discussing, as I understand. This resolution speaks of curing and canning. Everybody knows there is a great difference. It is quite right that there should be a license for canning food of any kind. But I cannot see why there should be a license -for curing fish by smoking, pickling, or otherwise. No license is exacted for this at the present time, and I do not see why there should be any.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: There has been a mistake in drafting the resolution. What was intended was the cannery license and not the fishing license, for we do not propose to compel the fishermen to pay a license. So, I would propose to strike out the word ' fishing ' in the eighth line of the resolution, and substitute the word ' cannery.'
Amendment agreed to.
I call special attention to this question of curing -fish. No license-should be imposed for this, and I must strongly oppose any such thing.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: Under the existing legislation, section 35 of the Fisheries Act, it is provided ' no one shall at any time can or cure,' and so on. Section 36 determines the license which is to be paid for canning or curing. The two words are used, and we propose to leave them as they are.
It is limited to salmon curing or canning.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: No, lobster curing or canning.

In that case, of course, the word ' curing ' in this connection means nothing, for there is no way of curing lobster except by canning. But from the resolution it might apply not only to British Columbia but to other provinces. In that case, the inclusion of the word ' curing ' would be of great interest to all who are interested in the fisheries of the maritime provinces or eastern Quebec, for in these places there is practically no salmon canned, it is all sold fresh, or cured by being smoked or otherwise. It would not be fair to ask the fishermen to procure a license for curing fish when the fish speaks for itself when it is presented to the customs.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The first part of the resolution deals with the cannery establishments of the province of British Columbia only, -and the latter part deals with lobster licenses and nominally covers the whole country, so, in practice it affects only the maritime provinces for only there are lobster canneries in existence. The first part of the resolution .uses the words ' curing or cannery,' but this applies only to British Columbia.

If that is settled, then, I have only a word in regard to the increase of the cost of the licenses. I take it that this license is not intended as a revenue producer, but is merely a nominal fee intended to give the government practical power of regulation. Of course, the increase quoted is not very great, but still it is an increase. Behind the lobster cannery is the lobster fisherman, and the higher you make the fixed expenses of the charges of the cannery, the less the establishment can afford to pay the fisherman. I would suggest that the minister should not increase that fee if he can see his way clear to do so. Then I would like to ask the minister how far we are going to increase these licenses, and whether we are going to do as was suggested in the Marine and Fisheries Committee, and as our fishermen desire, so that a man who catches a lobster will have the right to can that lobster if he wishes. For my part I never could see how a limitation of the number of canning factories, or any other kind of factory, was going to protect the fisheries. I can understand fish in the sea being protected by limiting the number of fishermen, or by using less destructive methods of fishing; but I never could understand how the limiting of the number of canning factories was going to preserve the fish in the sea. Therefore, I stand for as free a regulation as possible regarding the canning of lobsters. I think that a lessening of the number of factories would have no effect on lessening the catch, or on the yearly production of lobsters. When the number Mr. BRODEUR.
of factories is small they frequently force a man who catches a lobster at a -gertain port to -carry it to another port several miles away where he can ship it fresh. At the time of the change there were a number of factories located in different parts of Nova Scotia, and no doubt in Prince Edward Island a\jd New Brunswick, which, when this regulation came into force, simply closed up some of their factories, and said to the fishermen: If you want to sell your lobsters you must bring them to Charlottetown, or you must bring them to Canso, or you must bring them to Yarmouth. Therefore, the lobster fisherman was handicapped from the fact that competition was not keen enough. My hon. friend whom I see opposite is a canner of lobsters, and he knows what a nice thing it is to have that privilege exclusively. I do not blame him for that, but I am speaking for the mass of the fishermen generally. I do not forget the canner altogether, but he is quite able to take care of himself.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: I may tell my hon. friend that the monopoly he speaks of-
I would not call it a monopoly.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: But the restriction which exists in regard to lobster licenses has disappeared by the regulation we have adopted. This question engaged the consideration of the Committee on Marine and Fisheries, and they came to the unanimous conclusion that the restrictions which existed until then should disappear. In the last two years I have changed the regulations in that respect, as they are only departmental regulations, and I gave the privilege of acquiring a license to a number of fishermen combining together who applied for it. Several applications were made, and have been favourably considered. I will tell the reason why the increase was made, and I am voicing the unanimous finding of the Committee on Marine and Fisheries, of which I think my hon. friend is a member. That committee unanimously recommended 'that, in order to afford additional protection to the lobster fisheries, we should exact a little larger tax upon the canners. I suppose my hon. friend must he pleased to see that we are imposing a larger tax upon the canners, which was 'the unanimous recommendation of the committee.

I am not in any way opposed to the canner, I want him to get all the advantage he can. But I do say that if the canner has to pay $5 for a license, he is certainly going to take that out in the price he pays to the fishermen. But I wanted to know more particularly why this additional tax was put on, if it is not intended for revenue purposes, and I

do not think it can be. Why should we increase it at all? I think it would be better to leave it as it was before.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: It was in order to give additional protection to the fisheries.

I have a letter from Mr. John Berrigan, in the eastern part 'of Halifax county, who made application for a canning license to the overseer of fisheries there. Mr. Berrigan has written to me that he had not had any response to his application for some time. Perhaps the department would know whether that license has been granted.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries
speechtext: The superintendent informs me that he has not heard of any such application.

I will send the letter to the minister.

Mr. LEMIEUX moved the second reading of Bill (No. 104) to amend paragraph (1) of section 2, and paragraphs (n) and (o) of section 9 of the Post Office Act.
Will the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) be good enough to give a brief explanation of the nature of the proposed Bill?

Mr. Speaker, I have already given an explanation of the purpose of the Bill, but as it was given some weeks or even months ago, I will be pleased to repeat it. This is a Bill which will bring officially under the jurisdiction of the Post Office Department a new device called The Automatic Stamp Vending Machine. This automatic stamp vending machine has been in use in England, in Germany and in Australia for a certain number of years. I think the invention is an Australian one. The box can be well described, as it has been described by an authority on post offices in England, as a conscience stamp vending box. The reason why this box is called a conscience automatic stamp vending box is because, when you put a cent in the slot, if it is a false coin, the box rejects it. If it is not a current coin of the country it also rejects it, although it might be a good coin in the United States or in England. It is really a remarkable invention. The machine has been in use in Gieat Britain for a few years. It is aimed to facilitate the sale of stamps in large 255
establishments and in post offices to prevent any rush at the wickets where stamps ire sold. For instance, we have already placed in some of the post offices, at Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa, Vancouver and in some of the large hotels, some of these stamp vending machines and the result's have been simply marvellous. The benefits accruing from that invention are two-fold. First of all, it prevents a rush at the wickets in what are called rush seasons. At Christmas, it may be, or at Easter, when a huge number of cards and letters is sent through the mails, the public cannot afford to wait. Secondly, it saves to the Post Office Department the large commissions which are being paid to stamp vendors. That, I must say, is a secondary consideration because after all we must expect that those who sell stamps for His Majesty must be paid a certain commission. The purpose of the amendment herein is to enable the department to place at the service of the public, as experience -warrants, a device for the automatic sale of stamps. Let me take the first amendment to the Post Office Act. As my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is aware a postal box in the street is, according to the Post Office Act, a Post Office by itself. It is defined as such and when we have couriers who are charged with the responsibility of carrying the mails from one office to another, it often happens that on their route they have to take the mails from one, or two or three, or five of the boxes erected on the way. This stamp vending machine can be placed in the street and in the lobbies of large hotels, like the Windsor in Montreal, the Russell in Ottawa, or the new Grand Trunk hotel when it is opened, and in all the large hotels in the country. The moneys deposited in these boxes will be collected by our couriers under certain conditions that will be imposed by the department. Subsection (1) of section 2 defines a post office to embrace any building, room, post office, railway car, street letter box, &c., and the purpose of the amendment is to give street stamp vending boxes the same status. I hope I have made myself clear on that paragraph. Paragraph (n) of section 9 of the Post Office Act empowers the Postmaster General to establish and provide street letter boxes or boxes of any other description for the receipt of mailable matter whenever he deems it necessary and the purpose of the proposed amendment is to give the Postmaster General power to establish and provide boxes for the sale of stamps or other post office supplies whenever he deems it necessary. That is in order to see that the definition of the powers of the Postmaster General cover this additional case in the Post Office Department. Subsection (o) of



section 9 of the Post Office Department empowers the Postmaster General to grant licenses, revocable at pleasure, to agents other than regular postmasters for the sale to the public of postage stamps and standard envelopes. My hon. friends will know what standard envelopes mean. It happens that in the Post Office Department we sell to some large firms envelopes which are already stamped. This is in order to facilitate the business of large stores and it is very useful to the public. The purpose of this amendment is to allow of greater flexibility which will redound to the advantage of the department. These licenses, as stated in the section of the Post Office Act to which I refer, are revocable at pleasure. We wish to take away the words ' revocable at pleasure ' and for this very obvious reason.	.
The stamp vending boxes can be purchased by the. department, and placed here and there in the country; we have already purchased 50 as a trial, but our inspectors, and our superintendent of post offices, Mr. Ross, state that in certain sections of the country, especially where we have lumber camps, we may have difficulty in getting a regular post office, or even a regular agent for the sale of stamps to lumbermen. My officers say that we might well give the company which manufactures the boxes the privilege of installing those boxes in those remote sections of the country, the company to draw what commission we would pay to agents having stamp vending licenses. Of course the license will always be revocable whenever the Postmaster General, or the officers of the department find it necessary to revoke it, but the company state that they will have difficulty in establishing their business on a firm basis, if the words ' revocable at pleasure ' remain in the statute. I am explaining now the three amendments connected with this new machine. I must say that in the opinion of my officers this will be a great public utility. In our cities we have established some on trial, and the results have been simply marvellous. I have here a memorandum from one of my officers:
The Automatic Stamp-Vending Machines will not only prove a great convenience to the public, but in many cases, they meet an an actual necessity. They may be placed at any point where people require stamps in considerable numbers. They can be attached to pillar boxes on the street, in the halls of hotels, at railway stations, or in public buildings, and they are always available. Where access can be had to any of these machines, no person desiring to post a letter, and having the money to (buy a stamp, need go disappointed. At any hour of the day or night, at times when even the hotels or drug stores are no longer available, owing to the lateness of the hour, these machines are as Mr. LEMIEUX.
ready to do business with poople wishing to post letters as at mid-day. A very great advantage is that it fits in so completely with the habits of the people as regards correspondence. It is the universal practice to put off the posting of one's letters until the mail is ready to close. There is a rush to the stamp vendors, and in spite of every willingness to sell the stamps required, the vendor is unable to accommodate many, who apply to him. With automatic sellers near by, the situation is relieved for the vendor, and those desiring stamps are able to get what they want in time to post their letters to catch the outgoing mail.
In the principal cities of , Great Britain they are a boon to the public. There is a single box in Liverpool that sells on the average over 2,500 stamps a week, and another in Edinburgh from which the average issued is over 2,800 a week. In the crowded business sections of London, Glasgow, Dublin and Belfast, these automatic stamp sellers are doing thriving businesses to the great advantage of the public in these great centres of population. These machines are simple in construction and not liable to get out of order. One has been in use in the British House of Commons for two years, and has worked during all that time without a single failure.
A peculiar and very valuable feature, in these machines is that they reject, all spurious or foreign coins without operating the machine.	. '
In 1908, the parliament of Canada authorized the reduction of the rate on drop letters, that is, letters delivered in the city where they are posted; in cities, from 2 cents to one cent per ounce. This reduction has immensely increased the number of letters Pasted in our cities, and as a consequence the department is grateful for the opportunity which this device offers of serving the public better with the stamps which they want in such largely augmented numbers.	_
The machines have been set up experimentally in Ottawa, Montreal and, Toronto, and have given the utmost satisfaction. Two were placed in the exhibition building in Toronto during exhibition week and were worked at full pitch without a hitch. These machines quite outdid the British average mentioned. On one of the exhibition days, one machine sold 1,500 stamps, while a day or two later another machine sold 3,300 within 14 hours. The British high average, it will he remembered, were 2,500 and 2,800 in a week.
If a man wanted to buy a one cent stamp, and put in a five cent piece, would be get back four cents in change?
No, but from my own experience I can tell my hon. friend that if you put a 25 cent piece in, the machine wiil reject it.
Then I understand that this box does not give any change, but it is necessary to have the right com to put in the slot?
Yes.
What is the method of getting one of these boxes? For instance, suppose a hotel-keeper wanted one?

I intend to have special regulations for the leasing of these boxes. Of course, we must be very careful of them, because they are somewhat costly. We must for our climate have a strong metallic box, and we cannot give them away/ to every Tom, Dick and Harry. They are intended for the benefit of the public in large centres of population, at such rush centres as large hotels and railway stations, and also at remote points such ias lumber camps, where we have no agents. I had an application from a large firm in northern Ontario for one of these boxes, and I am just awaiting this legislation in order to place them in some of the lumber camps. It may be asked why we did not adopt a Canadian invention. The officials have been examining these machines for years, and they find the British pattern far the best. It is an Australian invention, and has been adopted by the British authorities and is used on the 'Continent in large centres.
Do I understand that only Canadian cents can be used?
Yes.
If a man put in five cents he would not get it back?

It would be returned to him, but he would not get any stamps. It is for one-cent and two-cent stamps- until the happy day comes when we shall require the half-cent stamp, as advocated by my hon. friend from Hatton.
I was just going to ask the minister whether he has made any provision for the half-cent stamp which we require in the towns?
