Before six o'clock I explained the various sections of the Bill, but if hon. members desire to ask any questions, I shall be glad to give any further information I can.
On section 1-'Street stamp vending box.'
It seems to me it would be proper to have a definition of the words 'street stamp vending box.'

We must provide something in the Act to bring this box under the purview of the Post Office Department. The ordinary post office box is a post office for the purpose of the Act, and we wish to have the same declared as regards to the stamp vending box.
So that, for instance, in case there should be a robbery it would come within the Act?
Yes.
How many of these vending machines are leased, and what amount of money is to be paid?

The machine is not leased but sold to the department. In certain cases machines are not under the entire supervision of the department. This applies to boxes located in distant districts, for instance in lumber camps. The Minister of Labour has several requests from people in lumber camps asking that they should be given the benefit of these boxes because nobody could be appointed postmaster in the deep recesses of our Canadian woods. The machines will be neither leased nor purchased by the department, but authority will be given to the company supplying the boxes to place them under our direction and the company will

be held to act as our agents. As my hon. friend is aware, each box is provided with -a roller of stamps. The company will buy the stamps from the department, and we will pay to the vendors the ordinary commission we pay to stamp vendors.
What is the cost of a box?

I think $25 is the cost of the box with one slot. But Dr. Coulter, the Deputy Postmaster General and Mr. Ross, of Toronto, have stated that the experiments we have made this winter with the boxes have shown that the public prefer the double box, one that will sell both one cent and two cent stamps. These double boxes cost about $40 or $50; I can give the exact figure on Monday.
How many does the minister intend to place?

We will have to create districts, and the demand, whatever it may be, will be met. The public desire to have devices to save time as much as possible. With the increase of population and the extraordinary expansion o'f letter writing, we have to meet that demand of the public. I do not say how many boxes. I suppose for the first year we will have two or three hundred. But at all events, we. will have a sufficient supply.
Is this a Canadian invention?

It is a British invention, and I said before six o'clock, that it was the best invention known up to date. That is the opinion of the British experts. At the same time, I may say for the benefit of Canadian inventors that we are not wedded to this particular box, and if they can find a better one we will adopt it. It is a conscientious box. We have never seen a box yet which would give back spurious coin or foreign coin. In this one, if you do not put in a Canadian penny or a Canadian cent, the box rejects it automatically. I intend to bring one of these boxes next week up to the House for the inspection of members. In Australia, in Germany, it has been adopted by the postal authorities. Last year when I was in Liverpool the postmaster showed me one of these boxes which collected, I do not know how many pounds a day.

The minister has told us about a machine which will sell stamps for the amount of money, one-cent or tw-o-cents, dropped into the box. Probably the minister knows that in the west there are no coppers nothing but silver money. I would ask him whether he has considered the need of a stamp vending machine that will sell stamps for a five cent piece or a Mr. LEMIEUX.
ten cent piece? There is perhaps greater need in the west of such a machine than in the east, for the reason that accommodation provided in the west in a very short time becomes inadequate, and something that would remove the congestion from the stamp vending wicket in the post office building would in a great many towns be much more of a necessity than it_ is in the east, on account of the more rapid development.

The object of this legislation is precisely to meet that contingency, namely, that in the west, and in cities where there is a rush at certain seasons, we may assist the post office authorities by placing this box in the lobbies. It helps them both in mailing letters, and it saves the government the commission we have been paying to vendors of stamps.-With regard to giving -change, this box is not adapted for that, but this is the latest device. If later on another better device is found which will sell stamps for a five or a ten cent piece, we will adopt it.
Has the minister committed himself to take this machine from only one particular firm, or may he purchase elsewhere if some other invention came out?

Certainly. We are not wedded, as I have said, to this_ particular automatic machine. I have simply described the latest machine as being the best one yet discovered. But if in the future a Canadian inventor-and there are many Canadians working in that line-discovers a better device, certainly we will adopt it. The same with the rural box. We have adopted the red box called the ' King Edward ' box, which, according to experts, is the best up to date box. But if a better one can be found we will _ certainly adopt it. At present the American authorities have accepted our rural box because they think it is the best.

I did not speak of a box that would return the change. What I had in mind was a machine which would return the stamps for five, ten or twenty-five cent piece thrown into it. In the west where we have no coppers, we cannot buy stamps in a less quantity than five cents worth.
Many men are working on this device daily, and if my hon. friend will come to the Post Office Department he will see a number of new devices.
The fact that this machine has a conscience will be no embarrassment to the government, I hope. Is there any way by which immoral literature can be rejected?

No, it does not deal *with literature.
On the preamble,

The Postmaster General will remember that for several years past I have drawn his attention to the fact that in the cities drop letters were reduced from two cents to one cent. This saving was given to those who reside in the cities where there is a street delivery, and I think it is only fair that in rural sections the people should be given an equivalent. I see no better way of doing it than for the minister to give the same reduction on drop letters to people living in country villages and towns that he gives to those living in the cities. The people in the cities have the benefit of a free delivery, but in the country the people have to go to the post office for their mail matter. Yet they have to pay the same postage on a drop letter that is paid in a city where the letter is delivered at the door of the person to whom it is addressed. The minister told me a year or two ago that after he had a year's experience in the working of the one cent drop letter in the cities, he would be prepared to consider the propriety of accepting or rejecting my proposition. I have waited now patiently for more than two years, and I think it is time the country people should get this little benefit. Merchants send out a great many circulars, and half a cent on each circular would, in the course of a year, amount to considerable money. You may say that the government wants the money, but the government is rich and the revenue is abundant. It seems to me that this is something that the Postmaster General might meet the demand of the country in, by giving a half cent rate to medical men, lawyers, merchants and any others who had occasion to mail a good many letters; in fact, give this reduction to any one. There will be no difficulty in buying half cent stamps. If a man could not get a half cent stamp he could buy two and use the new machine the minister might require to have an additional roler so as to turn out half cent stamps.
That difficulty could be got over.
That difficulty could be got over. Can the Postmaster General tell me if he can get over the other difficulty?
My hon. friend is very persistent in his efforts for further reduction of the postal rates.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon; in the rural section we have not had any reduction for a long time.
My hon. friend must not forget that when Sir William Mulock was in office some years ago, he reduced the rate from three cents to two.
But that did not apply to the one cent rate.

A further reduction was made three years ago by .myself for drop letters in cities. As to a half cent rate for the rural sections of the country, I may say to my hon. friend, without committing the government or any one, that I am seriously considering this question. Of course, it is a question of revenue and I must be very careful. I must be-well, let me say-conservative in this regard, but, when the proper time comes, if it is at all possible to meet the desires of the rural community, I will certainly be only too happy to grant the reduction. I am seriously considering the matter, but it is not one of the things that can be done in a haphazard way, and we must consider whether the reduction we are giving the people in, for instance, rural mail delivery, and other facilities which we provide, all of which must increase the expenditure, can be supplemented by a further reduction. It is true the revenues are abundant and increasing every year, but at the same time we must not lose sight of the fact that two cents is a very low rate. There is no country in the world where the people pay so little for the carriage of newspapers-one quarter of a cent a pound. Again I say I am studying this question with my officials. I know that the more you reduce the rates the more you are apt to get larger revenues. That is my experience, and that is why I have always been advocating a fair reduction of rates. It has meant for the Post Office Department larger revenues. If we had cheaper rates for cables I think that the cable companies would receive larger revenues. That is my policy and it is the experience of the experts we have ip the Post Office Department.

The minister refers to. the fact that in country places rural mail delivery is being introduced. But the reduction that I have referred to would have no connection with the rural mail delivery. Where I ask for a reduction is where a letter is dropped into the post office and taken out of the same post office, the Tesult being that the department is not put to any expense to carry it to any other place. I think the matter is a very simple one and one that should appeal especially to the Postmaster General. If he could reduced the postage to half a cent to such men as general merchants, I have no hesitation in saying that

he would find that he would get just as much 'revenue out of the half cent rate as out of the cent rate, because I believe they would make a great deal more use of the post office. I am glad to know that the minister has this under his serious consideration. I hope it will become more serious and it will not be long until we realize something out of it.

I desire to make a suggestion to the hon. Postmaster General which I hope he will also take under his favourable consideration. It is in regard to the correspondence which members of parliament have during recess. I do not know whether this matter has been brought to the minister's attention before, although I think that probably it has. I can see no reason why members of the House of Commons, carrying on correspondence during the recess upon public business, should not have the facilities of the mail just as well as during the time that the House of Commons is in session. If anything I believe that the correspondence of members in regard to public business is larger during the period of the recess, because, while the House of Commons is in session a member is in Ottawa and goes to the departments personally, and it is because he is away from Ottawa that the correspondence between himself and his constituents increases. I think the thing is right, and that it is in the interest of the member giving the best possible service to his constituents. It necessarily follows that if a member of parliament in carrying on correspondence with his people, has these facilities to which, I think, he has' a perfect right, they will get better service; not that_ any member is going to refrain from writing to his constituents for the sake of the cent or two postage that it may involve, and I do not know that it makes a great difference in that respect, but in this world with most men every dollar counts and it is scarcely fair to ask members to bear this charge themselves. It is nothing more than fair that the country should provide him with these facilities. Of course the question occurs as to how a man is going to draw the line. I do not think that any great practical difficulty is presented by that question. We know that in the United States they have a penalty envelope, that is an envelope Specially prepared for that purpose. I do not know that members of the House of Representatives or Senate use it, but I know that the Post Office Department does issue certain penalty envelopes which certain public officers residing away from the capital use. I do not know what the penalty is, it may be $40 or $50 for improper use, but that is immaterial to the principle of the thing.

I do not think that there will be any danger of members of parliament failing to correctly draw the line as between correspondence on public business and cor-responence on their own private business. As one who has a large correspondence- and I think all western members have, as I have no dloubt all members Jhave-I would suggest to the minister that it would be only doing what is fair, and following the principle that is already adopted while we are in Ottawa to make provision that members of parliament carrying on correspondence in connection with public business with their constituents should have the same facilities during twelve months in the year that they have while parliament is in session.
I will take the suggestion of my hon. friend under very serious consideration. Of course, it has no reference to the present Bill.

Is the minister aware that during the past few days there has been some slight interference with the mails that are coming to the House? I understand that a number of papers which should have been delivered this morning in the Library and in the Senate library did not arrive either by the morning or evening mail. Possibly the minister will make some investigation.

As my hon. friend is aware, the post office in the House of Commons is not under my jurisdiction. It is under the jurisdiction of the committee on internal economy. I am sorry to hear that there has been some mis-sent mail matter, but I will inquire. I found not very long ago that it took more time for a letter mailed in the House of Commons in the evening to reach the Post Office Department next morning than it took for a letter mailed in Montreal to reach my department. I saw the Speaker about it and found that the officers of the post office here closed the mails when the House adjourned, and the mails sometimes were sent only next morning from the Ottawa post office, while they could very well have been sent by the Toronto train until half past eleven at night, and the westbound train from Montreal passing through Ottawa about five o'clock in the morning. The Speaker was kind enough to call the postmaster, and to instruct him, with the help of one additional clerk, to keep the bag open until the early hours in the morning so as to give members the benefit of having their mails sent by those trains. As regards the error of this morning, I will inquire at once and see where the trouble lies.

A great many members of this House get copies of their

speeches from the Printing Bureau, where the type is already set up, for distribution through the post office. There is a provision in the regulations to this effect:
Members of either the Senate or the House of Commons may during the recess of parliament send by mail free of Canadian postage all papers printed by order of either House.
Will the minister inform me whether a member could during the recess send these copies of his speeches free of postage from the post office where he lives, in case he could not get them from the Bureau until after the House had prorogued.
There is another regulation which permits a member, within a certain time after prorogation, I think a fortnight, to mail public documents, blue-books, &c., from his home office.
I think he can do that all the year round.

As regards the case mentioned, I will look into it and see if I can accommodate the members in that respect. Of course, it is better to have the mailable matter sent in bulk from Ottawa, and distributed from here. If necessary, we can provide some regulation which would meet the contingency mentioned. The trouble is that it might be abused; but of course we must believe in the honour of every member of the House of Commons, and I think I can frame a regulation that would meet the case.
If we could have the King's Printer stamp his impress on the copies, then I am quite sure the present regulation would be sufficient.

I would like to call the minister's attention to a fraudulent use of the mails in western Ontario. In yesterday's London ' Free Press ' there is an article in which it is stated:
Letters are finding their way from the United States to all parts of Ontario, offering counterfeit money for sale. These 'green-goods' men choose farmers principally for their victims, and in the letters, picture 'easy money' that can be made if the recipient of the letter will communicate with the man who has the goods.
If the minister would call the attention of the authorities in western Ontario to this matter, it might be of some service.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

House went into committee on Bill (No. 167), respecting the inspection and sale of seeds.-Mr. Fisher.
On section 1,

This Bill was considered by the Committee on Agriculture, and with
the exception of one or two small amendments it passed that committee unanimously-	.
Is the Bill now as recommended by the Committee on Agriculture?

What is the object of exempting by the operation of sections 6 and 7, certain classes of persons mentioned in section 5?

Does the case mentioned this afternoon come within the meaning of
the Act, so that if the peeople sell wheat for seed, containing a certain percentage of weeds

?

Bill (No. 153) to amend the Inspection and Sale Act as regards the weight of a bushel and a bag of certain articles.-Mr. Fisher-read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon.
On section 1,
Would the minister explain what changes have been made?

Artichokes were not included in the original Act at all. Beans are the same, 60 lbs. to the bushel. Beets

were 60 lbs., and are now made 50. Bituminous coal is the same. Blue grass seed is the same, 14 lbs. Carrots were 60 in the old Act, and they are now made 50. Castor beans are the same. Clover seed is the same. Hemp seed was 49, and it is now made 44. Lime is the same, 70 lbs. Malt is the same, 36 lbs. Onions are the same, 50 lbs. Parsnips were 60, and are now made 45. Potatoes are the same, 60 lbs. Timothy seed is the same, 48 lbs. Turnips were 60 lbs., and are now made 50. All these changes were made at the request of the yegetable Growers' Associations of Ontario and Quebec. They explain that the weights in the old Act were so high that the ordinary measurement never came up to the weight. They say that the weights now adopted are reasonable, and are in accord with the ordinary measure of a bushel.

I understand that the weight of lime is left where it was before. Has the minister ever had any test made as to whether that is the correct weight of a bushel of lime? I remember it was formerly 80 lb's., and I think that was made at the suggestion of some member of the Senate, but it was reduced at my suggestion, and I was wondering whether the minister has ever had it confirmed.

I cannot say that I have officially. I have myself purchased lime and weighed it, and I know it was very rare that you could get a bushel of lime that weighed 80 lbs. I think 70 is the correct weight.

We had a test made in this way: I weighed a bushel of lump lime, and then took a bushel of fine lime and threw it in along with the larger pieces, and of course the smaller lime disappeared amongst the larger lumps, but, strange to say, it made no difference in the weight.
On subsection 2,
You provide that a bag of potatoes shall weigh 80 lbs., unless a bag by measure is specially agreed upon. Is that the legal standard?
There is no legal standard to-day for a bag of potatoes, except in the province of Ontario. This will make 80 lbs. the legal standard all over the Dominion.
The minister knows that 90 lbs is the correct weight.

I always expected to get 90 lbs. if I bought a bag. But at the same time it has been 80 in the province of Quebec for a long time, and now we make it 80 all over the Dominion. Many representa-Mr. FISHER.
tions were made, both to myself and to the Department of Trade and Commerce, asking that the weight be made 80 lbs.

Has 90 lbs. been the legal weight in Ontario?
Mr. FISHER There was no legal weight in Ontario.

I assume the min-siter knows why it was made 80 lbs.? In the province of Quebec it was made 80 lbs. because that was the weight of an ordinary bag of potatoes, and that weight was made to conform to the size of the bag. In Montreal I think they use a great many sugar bags, and the farmers who fill them with potatoes find that a bag will hold 90 lbs. So they made the weight 90 lbs. in order to conform to the size of the bag. Under our former legislation that weight was confined to the province of Quebec, and I am not sure but that it should be confined there still, and let 90 lbs. be the legal weight of a bag of potatoes.

There have been a good many smaller bags in use of late years in other parts of the country than Quebec. Strong representations were made from farmers outside of Quebec to reduce the weight of a bag of potatoes to 80 lbs. The legular two-bushel grain bag, which is the well known cotton grain bag, holds two bushels of grain, and will hold 90 lbs. of potatoes if it is well filled and shaken down. But there are many smaller bags used now, and grain is now nearly all sold by weight without reference to bags. Grain is now put into any kind of a bag, whereas it used to be put generally into a two-bushel bag. Now bags vary in size. I know they are with us and I think they are all over the country. There is no fixed standard of capacity for a bag and it, therefore, has been thought well by people who are interested in this trade that a bag of these different things should have a fixed weight. It is proposed that a bag of potatoes shall be 80 lbs.

The invariable rule has been that a bag of any kind of roots or fruit should be a bushel and a half. Now you depart from that with regard to a great many of the articles that are mentioned in this list. It will deceive the public greatly if this change is made. The change with regard to the weight of a bag of potatoes is a very drastic one.

The only standard that there ever has been for a weight of a bag of any of these articles has been with respect to a bag of potatoes in the province of Quebec. Until now there has been no standard weight for bag of any of these articles.
What was the practice?

It varied in different parts of the country. I think that in Ontario a bag of potatoes was usually a bushel and a half, or 90 pounds, and in other parts of the country it was not. In the maritime provinces I believe it was 75 pounds, while in Quebec, by the law of the land, it was 80 pounds. These people have requested that it be made uniform all over the country at 80 pounds.
As far as potatoes are concerned, it is going to lead to very serious difficulty as between buyers and sellers if that rule is adopted.

I agree with my hon. friend from Durham (Mr. Thornton). The standard rule in the province of Ontario, as long as I can remember, has been 90 pounds for a bag of potatoes. The minister says that the ordinary cotton bag used on the farms has to be filled up and well shaken down to hold 90 pounds of potatoes. He has evidently not weighed many potatoes in ordinary cotton bags, because they do not require to be shaken down to get a weight of 90 pounds. But there is a flour bag which is used on the farms, and in order to put 90 pounds into that it has to be shaken down and tied very closely. It will cause a great deal of confusion for some time, throughout Ontario, at least, where the public have been so accustomed to dealing in a 90-pound bag of potatoes, if you adopt 80 pounds as the standard bag it will practically compel the farmer, who sells a bag of potatoes as a bag, to sell by weight. The old standard measure of a bushel and a half to the bag was considered correct, and no doubt was correct. In our pjart of the country they buy potatoes by the bag at 90 pounds, and it will cause confusion if you bring about this change.

These weights have beeni fixed upon representations of people interested who have come to us from time to time. A delegation came down to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce in regard to this Bill, and these are the weights fixed upon by them. I have received a great' many representations in the way of correspondence which I have transferred to the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because, this being an amendment to the Inspection and Sale Act, it comes under his department. I have had a great many representations from different parts of the country, a good many, I think, from Ontario. I do not remember* just now where they all came from, but I am sure that some came from Ontario, asking for this change.
Who comprised thq deputation?
They called themselves the vegetables growers of Ontario and the vegetables growers of Quebec.
Not farmers?
No, they were not farmers.
Were the dealers interested in the same way?

I think the dealers would be in that deputation. This will not hurt the farmer. It is the purchaser, not the farmer, that will be hurt, if anybody is hurt, because the farmer will be able to sell 80 pounds as a bag in future instead of 80.
The only objection I can see to it is that it will cause confusion and hard feeling between buyer and seller.
Of course, it may take* a little time for the new standard to be understood, but evidently there has been a very positive request for this from the people who seem to be concerned in the trade.

I do not see that it is a great detriment to the farmer, but hundreds of thousands of people will be buying potatoes all over Ontario, they will not know that this new standard has been fixed for the next five years, and they will think that they are getting 90 pounds when they buy potatoes from the grocer, whereas they are only getting 80 pounds.

Will they not soon adjust themselves to the new conditions? It does take a good sized measure of potatoes to weigh 90 pounds. As a matter-of fact, dealers will accustom themselves to this change, and the price will be fixed accordingly.
These weights were also submitted to the officers of the Experimental Farm, Messds. Grisdale and Maeoun, and they tested and approved them.
How would they test the weight of a bag? They could test the weight of a bushel, but I do not know how they could test the weight of a bag of 80 pounds.
What measures did they use in testing the bag?
Of course, for the bushel, they took the regular bushel measure. The first part of this clause provides for the weight of a bushel. I do not know how they tested the weight of the bag.
What is the size of the bushel with which they made this test?
It is the regular standard bushel. The Inspection and Sale Act says what the bushel is.
2,142 inches, is it not?
I am not sure.

I can understand that if you provide for the use of the bushel measure in filling the bag, it will work all right, but if you do not I am afraid it will result in a great deal of inconvenience. A farmer will not be able to determine very accurately what quantity of potatoes he has in his sack except by having a pair of scales on the farm. A bushel measure is a very cheap article, and he can easily determine the quantity of potatoes that he is putting in the bag with the aid of the bushel measure.

He requires to use scales just as much now as he will if this Bill is passed. The standard of practice in the province of Ontario, I believe, has been 90 pounds, and the 90 pounds is now required as absolutely as the 80 pounds will be.

I think this may cause great confusion, and that great publicity should be_ given to the changes made before the Act is put into operation. The coming into force of the Act should be postponed until some future day, perhaps a year from next January.
The proposition to postpone the coming into force of the Act is a reasonable one, but I think that next January would be a sufficient delay.
The other would be only one crop of potatoes.
Does it fix the weight of a bushel of apples?

No. I would suggest that we should pass the other clauses of the Bill which are not controversial and leave it in committee until I have an opportunity of consulting the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the question of deferring the coming into operation of the Bill. I have not had charge of the drafting of the Bill.
We should have some definite promise that it will not be brought into force until the 1st of January.

I cannot promise that myself.
On section 2, existing Act repealed,

The royal assent was given during this session Jo a Bill introduced by the hon. member for Carleton, N.B., (Mr. Carvell) fixing the weight of a barrel of potatoes at 165 pounds. The Minister of Trade and Commerce thought it best to include that enactment under this Bill, and so avoid confusion, and this has been done. This fixes the standard at that weight.
What is the legal weight of a bag of potatoes in the United States? .
I do not know.
If we are framing our legislation on the American legislation in this matter, we should know just what their standards are.
I shall find that out.
Eighty pounds to a bag, and 165 pounds to a barrel seems inconsistent.

I do not think there is any interchange between the bag and the barrel.
On section 3, weight of barrel.
You determine the size of the barrel by the number of pounds. Could you not give the capacity of the barrel by giving the height, and the diameter at the top and middle as with apple barrels?

The reason that the size of the apple barrel is fixed by measurement is that apples vary greatly in weight, according to variety. The summer varieties of apples weigh 10 pounds per barrel less than the winter varieties. That difference does not exist with potatoes.
How is a man buying a barrel of potatoes to know that it id a legal barrel?

If he had any suspicion he would have to weigh it.
Progress reported.
Bill (No. 85) respecting forest reserves and parks, read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The major portion of the provisions of this Bill are already contained in the Forest Reserves Act. The most important differences between the Bill and the Act are that provision is made for placing all present forest and park reservations under the provisions of the Forest Reserves Act, and then setting apart, within those forest reservations, park reservations with regard to which the regulations look to the enjoyment by the people of the natural advantages and beauties ol those particular sections of the reserves, while the regulations regarding the remainder of the forest reserves look rather to the exclusion of people from them.

Will the hon. minister pardon me? I think this is too important a Bill to proceed with in so thin a House. I do not see the men here on either side who are sufficiently acquainted

with the matter dealt with in this Bill to deal with it intelligently, and we might as well leave it entirely in the minister's hands and let him put it through himself. If he has some other measure of less importance, I would suggest that he take it up and let this stand to come up in a full House earlier in the day. .

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I quite appreciate the point of view of my hon. friend, and I do not wish to minimize the importance of the Bill. I would like to say another word. Besides the provisions which I have mentioned, there is another important feature of the Bill. It sets apart by legislation the .Rocky Mountain Park Reserve, extending .along the eastern slope of the Rocky Mountains from the boundary until it is crossed by the boundary between British Columbia and Alberta '
Will it be entirely in Alberta?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. There is a reservation over a great deal of that country, by order in council passed last year; but since that time a careful examination has been made for the purpose of drawing what might be called a fairly scientific boundary between what is properly the park and what is not the park, and this Bill asks that this new boundary be adopted as the boundary of the park which will be set apart by legislative enactment.
Has the Conservation Commission recommended this Bill or been consulted in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Conservation Commission recommended the setting apart of the reserve on the whole of the eastern slope of the Rocky Mountains, and the Bill is in accordance with that recommendation. I am not aware that the commission made recommendations in regard to any other section of the Bill, because the Act now on the statute-book, which this Bill follows, with the exceptions I have mentioned, was in force before the Conservation Commission came into existence.
Does this Bill interfere with the present boundaries of the Duck Mountains reserve, the Riding Mountains reserve or the Turtle Mountains reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was going to say that besides that reservation, which will include the present reserves of the Kootenay Lakes park, the Rocky Mountains park at Banff, and the Jasper park, a careful examination of the other reserves created by the Act of 1906 has been made, and as a result of that examination there have been some alterations in the boundaries, which I would of course be prepared to state to the House at length. There have been some considerable additions made, in some cases small portions have been taken out of the reserves, and in one case, the Manitoba reserve has been dispensed with altogether, and a considerable area of the Donald Forest reserve it has been decided to throw open to settlement. The legislative features of the Bill are not important, as they do not differ materially from the provisions of the Act now on the statute-book. At the same time, I do not wish to minimize the desirability of the full House having a complete understanding of the Bill, and therefore, in deference to my hon. friend, I would move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Has the minister any map of the proposed reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I have a map which shows all the reserves, with all the alterations and additions, which I can leave on the table for the information of the House between now, and the future consideration of the Bill.
Do these reserves on the eastern slope of the Rocky Mountains comprise pretty nearly all the eastern water-shed of the Rockies?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I think they do. In setting apart the reservation we were guided by the principle that land at an elevation of 4,000 feet and over was not suitable for agricultural purposes, though it could still be used for grazing, because the grazing right does not involve alienation of the surface.
It is not intended to dispose of the timber on the reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is not open to the ordinary demand for timber, but the timber is to be disposed of at the option and on the responsibility of the department when it is mature. The idea is that the timber shall be administered with a view to preservation reproduction rather than to profit but it is not at all intended that the timber shall not be used.
Progress reported.

On order for second reading of Bill (No. 107) to amend the Dominion Lands Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is a Bill for making minor amendments to the Dominion Lands Act, which authorizes the leasing of school lands for revenue purposes towards the school funds. Up to the present time we have been leasing school lands, and there is a question as to our statutory authority to do so. It was thought well to make statutory provision to that end, and a clause was prepared for that purpose. Since, notice was given of this Bill, circumstances have arisen that have made it desirable to secure certain other minor amendments to the Act. I now wish to withdraw this Bill, and at the same time to give notice of the introduction of another Bill of the same name, but which would contain certain other additional provisions, in all cases making minor amendments which are considered necessary to the successful operation of the Act. I move, therefore, that Order 18 for the second reading of Bill (No. 107) be discharged.
Motion agreed to.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: In the French version of the Revised Statutes, clause 252, the word * huit ' has been substituted for the word ' quatre.' The consequence is to impose an inland revenue tax of eight cents per gallon instead of four cents. We wish to use the word ' quatre.' This section also amends the French version of section 356 of the said Act by inserting after the word ' loi ' in the sixth line thereof, the words ' est eoupable d'un acte criminal et,' which words have been left out of the Act.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext:
I was much surprised to see in the report of the Secretary of State so extraordinary a number of errors made in the French version of the statutes. I cannot understand why they should occur so frequently. I think there were in that report two pages of errors in

recent statutes. It does seem a remarkable thing that the word ' huit ' should be substituted for the word ' quatre ' in the French version, and it seems equally remarkable that the very important phrase which the minister has quoted should be left out at the end of a section. I would like to know the meaning of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: There is only one explanation, that is defective translation.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: It is not a translation at all when these important words are left out. But what I cannot understand is how they should occur so frequently.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: I cannot account for it on any other theory than, carelessness somewhere, and I suppose on the part of the translators.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: It seems important that whatever authority is charged with the supervision on this work should see that greater care is used in making the translation. Perhaps the Secretary of State can tell us how it is that these errors occur.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: I cannot give my hon. friend any other information than what he possesses. If there are errors in the printing, it is the fault of the printer.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: Some of these errors are attributed in some way to the Printing Bureau. The Secretary of State will Temember that in his report there is a long list of errors, I think two pages. I do not know whether they are attributable to the translators or to the Printing Bureau.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: They are attributable to the translators, and they were discovered by the officials of the Printing Bureau in Tending the proof.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: Are the English and French editions of these statutes issued simultaneously?

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: Almost.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: After they are printed, is anybody in a position to compare the two versions and see that they have been printed identically? Is there any system by which these translations are compared? We should not be running the risk of sending out two laws disagreeing with each other.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext:
The question raised by the member for St. Anne is an important one. Are the statutes passed in this parliament in English and French at the same time, or are they passed in English and a French translation made
afterwards? Is there an English version and a French version of statutes at the time they pass this House, and the Senate, and at the time they receive the assent of the Governor in Council? It seems to me that is what should be done. Both languages are the languages of legislation in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: Bills of course are always required to be printed in both languages, and in practice they are. So that at the time, parliament enacted it with that general amendment. I should think that there is no reason why these should not be published in both languages at the same time. Mr. Speaker, who has the supervision of this matter, informs me that he will have a memorandum prepared giving an [DOT]explanation of this error, and that he will be able to bring it before the House on some future occasion. There is no doubt that is a clerical error in translation.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: This appears to be a Bill to amend the revised statutes of 1906 for the purpose of correcting an error that has occurred in the French version. I would like to ask the minister when it was that this error was discovered, when he first knew of it and why this delay has occurred in bringing in this amendment to make the necessary correction?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: Personally I have only known of it for the last six months. The Deputy Minister called my attention to it six months ago and he thought it was necessary to amend the French version. How long my deputy has known of it I do not know.

maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext: They have been paying eight cents?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
maintopic: ERRORS IN FRENCH VERSION OF INLAND REVENUE ACT.
speechtext:
No; four cents.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.

speechtext: Consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 97) to prohibit the improper use of opium and other drugs.- Mr. King.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: What are the amendments?

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext:
These amendments do not affect in any way the principle of the Bill. The first amendment is the insertion of the words ' shall be guilty of a criminal offence ' in a number of the sections. The law as it stands states that a person doing

certain things shall be liable to summary conviction and to a certain fine. The senators thought that it would be just as well to put in the words ' shall be guilty of a criminal offence.' I do not think that they are absolutely necessary, but the Senate seems to think that they . will make the meaning clearer and as the prevention of certain evils is the object sought their insertion of these words is in line with the purpose of the Bill I do not see that there can be any objection to it. The second .amendment is to section 5 of the Bill, and it is the insertion of the words ' or to a bona fide wholesale druggist ' after the word ' dentist ' in the 15th line. Section 5 prohibits the sale of certain drugs to any person other than a physician, veterinary surgeon or dentist, except upon conditions prescribed by the Act. It seemed advisable to the Senate to allow the same privilege, in the matter of sale, to a bona fide wholesale druggist and, therefore, they inserted these woris.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: Would not the words ' a druggist carrying on business in a bona fide drag store ' cover that?

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: A wholesale druggist might not have any drug store at all; he might simply have a place of business and for that reason he comes within a different category. The remaining amendment is to the schedule. The Act specifies certain drugs in the schedule which it shall be unlawful to sell except under certain conditions. These drugs are cocaine, morphine and opium. The Senate thought it well to add, after the words * cocaine ' and ' morphine,' the words ' or any salts or compounds thereof.' That addition was made on the advice of the medical adviser of the Conservation Commission and also on the advice of the director general of public health. The intention of parliament in inserting cocaine and morphine was to deal with these two particular drugs and it was felt that unless the words ' or any salts or compounds thereof ' were added a violation of the intention of the Act might result. Then, the Senate provide in addition the words ' eucaine or any salts or compounds thereof.' Eucaine is a comparatively new drug much the same as cocaine and has much the same effect. It is in the nature of a powder which, I believe, is snuffed by people who use it and which has the same destructive effect as cocaine and opium. As these amendments, and particularly the last one, strengthen the Bill, and as they carry out the intention of this House, I am of opinion that they should be agreed to.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: Are these not covered by section 14?

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: No; section 14 says that the Governor in Council may add to the schedule of this Act any alkaloids, derivatives or preparations of the drugs named. Eucaine is not one of the drugs named. On the other hand I suppose that any salts or compounds of the drugs named could be added by order in council, but they are I think better specified comprehensively in the Act itself. The Senate thought it better to specify salts and compounds generally in the Bill.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: The section which I have here says that the Governor in Council may add any compounds or substances.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: The hen. gentleman has the Bill as introduced but not as passed. The Bill as passed was changed in some particulars. We confined the list of drugs to cocaine, morphine and opium.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: I suppose that we can assume that the senators all know what eucaine is, because I must confess that I have no knowledge what it is.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext: The suggestion has come from the medical adviser of the Conservation Commission which has to do, enough other things with the conservation of human resourses.

Amendments agreed to.
